javascript-foundations.check: Check that one action does not register duplicate handlers.

javascript-foundations.title: Debugging
javascript-foundations.teaching: Debugging compares actual behavior with a prediction and narrows possible causes. A logged value is evidence about that point in execution, not the entire program.
javascript-foundations.practice: A fictional total is wrong. Inspect its inputs and one intermediate result before changing the calculation.
javascript-foundations.check: Record the smallest reproducible failing example.

javascript-foundations.title: Testing cases
javascript-foundations.teaching: Conditions, input checks, and debugging provide different ways to examine a program. Tests should include ordinary, boundary, and invalid inputs.
javascript-foundations.practice: For a rule accepting ages 18 and above, propose tests for 17, 18, and nonnumeric input and predict each result.
javascript-foundations.check: An invalid input should not silently pass the rule.

javascript-foundations.title: Coding project
javascript-foundations.teaching: A small project connects data, a function, and a user interaction. Keeping these responsibilities clear makes behavior easier to explain and test.
javascript-foundations.practice: Plan a fictional task counter with one click handler and a function that computes the next count.
javascript-foundations.check: Check initial state, one click, and repeated clicks.

data-spreadsheets.title: Data questions
data-spreadsheets.teaching: A summary answers a particular question about specified records. Define the unit and time period before calculating a result.
data-spreadsheets.practice: Ask how many fictional applications were submitted this week rather than which week was best.
data-spreadsheets.check: State which records belong in the answer.

data-spreadsheets.title: Rows and columns
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Rows represent records and columns represent fields in a well-structured list. Consistent headings and data types make sorting and filtering dependable.
data-spreadsheets.practice: Create fictional columns for Application ID, Submitted date, and Status, with one application per row.
data-spreadsheets.check: Do not combine unrelated values in one field.

data-spreadsheets.title: Field definitions
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Consistent field meaning matters for both filtering and matching. Decide whether a date means submission, appointment, or completion before entering it.
data-spreadsheets.practice: Two fictional rows use Date for different events. Rename the fields so comparisons use the same event.
data-spreadsheets.check: Check the field definition before combining records.

data-spreadsheets.title: Data entry checks
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Data validation restricts accepted input according to a chosen rule. It reduces avoidable entry errors but does not prove the real-world information is true.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional Status field allows Draft, Submitted, or Closed. Explain rejecting an unrecognized value and checking the source.
data-spreadsheets.check: Validation is a control, not factual verification.

data-spreadsheets.title: Cleaning duplicates
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Sorting and filtering help inspect related records. Similar-looking rows may represent separate events, so deletion requires a defined matching rule.
data-spreadsheets.practice: Two fictional entries share a name but have different application IDs. Explain why deleting one solely by name loses information.
data-spreadsheets.check: Preserve the original data while reviewing candidates.

data-spreadsheets.title: Missing values
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Blank cells can complicate analysis and grouping. Missing is not automatically the same as zero or not applicable.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional survey has an unanswered income field. Explain marking it missing rather than entering zero for convenience.
data-spreadsheets.check: State how missing values affect the summary.

data-spreadsheets.title: Useful formulas
data-spreadsheets.teaching: A formula refers to cells or ranges and calculates from their contents. Check the intended range and input types before trusting the displayed total.
data-spreadsheets.practice: Explain =SUM(B2:B4) for fictional values 10, 15, and 5, and compare with a manual total.
data-spreadsheets.check: Expected result: 30; confirm that B2, B3, and B4 are the intended three inputs.

data-spreadsheets.title: Conditional logic
data-spreadsheets.teaching: IF returns different results based on a logical test. Testing a threshold and values on both sides reveals common comparison mistakes.
data-spreadsheets.practice: For =IF(B2>=3,"Ready","Review"), predict the result when B2 contains 2 and when it contains 3.

data-spreadsheets.title: Lookup concepts
data-spreadsheets.teaching: A lookup uses a key to find a related value. An exact-match setting matters when an approximate result could attach information to the wrong record.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional employee ID must match exactly. Explain why a nearby ID is not an acceptable substitute.
data-spreadsheets.check: Check the key and treatment of unmatched records.

data-spreadsheets.title: Pivot summaries
data-spreadsheets.teaching: A pivot table groups source records to calculate summaries. The selected field operation determines whether it counts records or adds amounts.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional application table has Status and Fee columns. Contrast counting applications by status with summing fees.
data-spreadsheets.check: Verify the source range and summary operation.

data-spreadsheets.title: Charts and scales
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Charts display a selected set of values. Labels and scales influence the comparison, and a polished chart can still use the wrong range.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional bar chart leaves out the lowest month. Describe checking the range and axis before interpreting it.
data-spreadsheets.check: Compare plotted values with the original cells.

data-spreadsheets.title: Percentages
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Percentage calculations need a denominator. A change between percentages can be expressed in percentage points or relative percent, with different meanings.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional completion rate changes from 40% to 50%. Explain the increase as ten percentage points or 25% relative to 40%.
data-spreadsheets.check: Always name the starting value and denominator.

data-spreadsheets.title: Privacy and minimization
data-spreadsheets.teaching: A usable table does not need every detail about a person. TCF applies the source's structured-field idea with data minimization and the lesson's privacy guidance.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional attendance summary needs counts, not addresses. Identify the fields needed for the question and omit the rest.
data-spreadsheets.check: Use only an authorized, appropriately limited dataset.

data-spreadsheets.title: Findings and limits
data-spreadsheets.teaching: Formula auditing traces which inputs feed a result. A calculation can be internally consistent while its data or interpretation remains incomplete.
data-spreadsheets.practice: A fictional report total is correct but excludes a missing week. Explain checking the range and stating the coverage limit.
data-spreadsheets.check: Separate arithmetic accuracy from data completeness.

data-spreadsheets.title: Data project
data-spreadsheets.teaching: A data project needs a defined question, structured records, a checked summary, and a stated limitation. The result should be reproducible by another reader.
data-spreadsheets.practice: Plan a fictional application-status summary and name the source range, calculation, and one missing-data concern.
data-spreadsheets.check: Retain a clean source copy and document changes.

responsible-ai.title: What AI generates
responsible-ai.teaching: Generative AI creates outputs that can appear fluent while being inaccurate. Presentation quality and factual reliability are separate properties.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional answer invents an organization name. Describe checking the claim rather than accepting its confident tone.

responsible-ai.title: Task suitability
responsible-ai.teaching: Task suitability depends on the intended outcome, affected people, reliability needs, and human accountability. Some decisions require qualified review rather than automated acceptance.
responsible-ai.practice: Compare drafting a fictional meeting agenda with deciding someone's eligibility for housing.
responsible-ai.check: Keep consequential decisions with the authorized reviewer.

responsible-ai.title: Clear prompts
responsible-ai.teaching: Traceable work records the inputs and conditions used to produce an output. A clear task, context, and output format make a draft easier to evaluate.
responsible-ai.practice: Specify a fictional audience, purpose, length, and source boundary for an email draft without adding personal data.
responsible-ai.check: A clear prompt still requires output review.

responsible-ai.title: Source verification
responsible-ai.teaching: Traceability connects outputs to inputs and evidence. A model-generated citation must be opened and checked before it supports a claim.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional AI draft cites a report that cannot be located. Explain removing or verifying the claim through the actual source.
responsible-ai.check: Do not treat a formatted reference as evidence.

responsible-ai.title: Privacy boundaries
responsible-ai.teaching: Data governance includes controlling access and protecting information. A tool's convenience does not establish permission to upload private records.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional user wants to paste a client's case notes into an AI tool. Describe using an approved workflow and minimizing data first.
responsible-ai.check: Do not enter actual private records in this exercise.

responsible-ai.title: Editing drafts
responsible-ai.teaching: Human review remains part of a responsible workflow. Editing should check meaning, unsupported additions, tone, and the intended audience, not just spelling.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional draft adds a guarantee the sender never made. Explain removing it and verifying all remaining commitments.
responsible-ai.check: Review the exact version that will be used.

responsible-ai.title: Learning with AI
responsible-ai.teaching: AI literacy includes understanding limitations and keeping human judgment involved. Learning is strengthened by explaining and testing an answer rather than copying it.
responsible-ai.practice: Ask for a fictional worked example, then identify and check one step independently.
responsible-ai.check: Be able to explain the result without the tool.

responsible-ai.title: Bias and assumptions
responsible-ai.teaching: Bias can arise through data, design, and use. Fairness review asks who is represented, excluded, or affected; a neutral-sounding sentence can still rely on a stereotype.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional draft assumes all returning citizens need the same support. Identify the assumption and rewrite it around individual needs.
responsible-ai.check: Check the effect on the people described.

responsible-ai.title: Job-search support
responsible-ai.teaching: Accountability means a person remains responsible for the final use of an output. A polished job-search draft should describe actual skills and experience.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional AI resume invents a certification. Explain removing the claim and checking the remaining qualifications.
responsible-ai.check: Never add a credential merely because it improves the draft.

responsible-ai.title: Spreadsheet assistance
responsible-ai.teaching: Data quality and reliability matter when AI suggests analytical work. A formula must be tested against known inputs, including difficult cases.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional tool suggests a spreadsheet total. Compare its range with the intended records and calculate a small sample manually.
responsible-ai.check: A plausible formula can reference the wrong cells.

responsible-ai.title: Creative rights
responsible-ai.teaching: The handbook flags legal compliance and accountability without resolving every creative-rights issue. Apply the lesson's rights guidance by checking permission and provenance before reuse.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional AI image resembles a protected logo. Explain seeking an appropriate original or licensed asset instead of assuming unrestricted use.
responsible-ai.check: Generation alone does not establish reuse permission.

responsible-ai.title: Automation boundaries
responsible-ai.teaching: Autonomy concerns how much control a system has, while accountability identifies who owns decisions and redress. External actions need clear human approval boundaries.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional automation drafts customer messages. Describe keeping sending behind an authorized review step.
responsible-ai.check: Define which actions the tool may actually perform.

responsible-ai.title: Recognizing uncertainty
responsible-ai.teaching: Reliability includes recognizing when an output is uncertain or unsupported. Repetition can expose inconsistency but does not by itself verify a fact.
responsible-ai.practice: Two fictional AI answers give different dates. Describe checking the primary source instead of choosing the more confident answer.

responsible-ai.title: Output evaluation
responsible-ai.teaching: Evaluation should match the intended task and include reliability, privacy, fairness, and usefulness. One successful demonstration does not establish dependable performance.
responsible-ai.practice: A fictional draft is readable but includes private data. Explain why it fails review despite its good style.
responsible-ai.check: Evaluate every required condition, not just convenience.

responsible-ai.title: Responsible workflow
responsible-ai.teaching: A responsible workflow defines purpose, allowed data, evidence checks, review ownership, and a way to report problems. Governance should be practiced, not only written down.
responsible-ai.practice: Plan a fictional draft-review-use sequence with a named human decision point and a correction record.
responsible-ai.check: Retain enough permitted context to explain the decision.

digital-literacy.title: Device vocabulary
digital-literacy.teaching: Hardware is physical equipment; software supplies instructions. Identify the device, application, and intended task separately before asking for help.
digital-literacy.practice: A learner calls a browser a computer. Separate the laptop, operating system, and browser in a three-item list.
digital-literacy.check: Can another person identify all three without guessing?

digital-literacy.title: Operating systems
digital-literacy.teaching: An operating system manages device resources and provides the environment for applications. Similar-looking icons do not prove two devices have identical settings.
digital-literacy.practice: Compare where two fictional devices store a downloaded document; describe the location rather than assuming identical menus.
digital-literacy.check: Name the system before choosing instructions.

digital-literacy.title: Keyboard and touch skills
digital-literacy.teaching: Input tools let a user select, enter, and revise information. Accuracy comes before speed; accessibility settings can change the input method.
digital-literacy.practice: A form contains a mistyped telephone digit. Describe selecting and replacing that digit, then reading the complete number back.
digital-literacy.check: Check the value rather than the typing speed.

digital-literacy.title: Files and folders
digital-literacy.teaching: File organization connects a meaningful name with a known location. A folder groups related resources; an application is not the same thing as the document it opens.
digital-literacy.practice: Name a fictional resume Resume-2026-10-15 and identify the folder where it belongs, keeping private identifiers out of filenames.
digital-literacy.check: Can the file be found again from its location?

digital-literacy.title: Saving and backups
digital-literacy.teaching: Digital resource management includes local and cloud storage. Saving a working copy and retaining a recoverable backup address different risks.
digital-literacy.practice: A resume exists only on one phone. Describe a second authorized storage location and a safe way to confirm the copy opens.
digital-literacy.check: A copy that cannot be opened is unverified.

digital-literacy.title: Browser basics
digital-literacy.teaching: Finding online information requires evaluating the source and purpose, not merely entering search terms. A browser displays a page; a search result points toward it.
digital-literacy.practice: Compare an official service page with an advertisement offering the same service. Identify who operates each destination.
digital-literacy.check: Inspect the destination before entering information.

digital-literacy.title: Downloads and uploads
digital-literacy.teaching: Uploading sends a local file to another system; downloading retrieves a copy. File selection, destination, and sharing permissions all matter.
digital-literacy.practice: An application requests a resume but the learner selects a banking statement. Describe canceling and checking the filename before submission.
digital-literacy.check: Check both the chosen file and recipient.

digital-literacy.title: Account recovery
digital-literacy.teaching: Account access is part of digital safety. Recovery information should remain under the account holder's control, rather than depend on a stranger's account.
digital-literacy.practice: A shared email address is offered as a recovery method. Explain why an account-controlled method and provider instructions are better.
digital-literacy.check: Never disclose a recovery code in a discussion.

digital-literacy.title: Password management
digital-literacy.teaching: Security measures protect access to digital information. Unique passwords and multifactor authentication address different weaknesses; one does not replace the other.
digital-literacy.practice: Two fictional services share a password. Describe replacing the reused secret and enabling an available additional factor.
digital-literacy.check: Practice without writing an actual password here.

digital-literacy.title: Accessibility tools
digital-literacy.teaching: Technology should support the user's task. Input, display, and reading supports can reduce barriers without changing the learning goal.
digital-literacy.practice: A learner cannot comfortably read a form. Compare zoom, text size, and a reading tool before deciding the form is unusable.
digital-literacy.check: Check that labels and controls remain usable.

digital-literacy.title: Storage awareness
digital-literacy.teaching: Local and cloud resources can have different capacity and access conditions. Deleting an unfamiliar file is not a sound first response to a storage warning.
digital-literacy.practice: A device reports low space. Identify the storage location and review known duplicates before proposing deletion.
digital-literacy.check: Retain a recoverable copy of important work.

digital-literacy.title: Updates and restarts
digital-literacy.teaching: Troubleshooting is a structured problem-solving task. Observe the symptom, identify the affected component, and use an authorized next step.
digital-literacy.practice: An update prompt appears during unsaved work. Describe saving the work and checking the provider's restart instructions.
digital-literacy.check: Record the symptom and result of the restart.

digital-literacy.title: Troubleshooting basics
digital-literacy.teaching: Decomposition means separating a problem into manageable parts. It helps distinguish an input error from an application or connection problem.
digital-literacy.practice: A form will not submit. Check one required field, then the connection, rather than changing everything at once.
digital-literacy.check: Say which test changed the result.

digital-literacy.title: Digital service forms
digital-literacy.teaching: Responsible digital participation combines accurate information with privacy. A legitimate-looking form still needs its purpose and operator checked.
digital-literacy.practice: A service form asks for optional information unrelated to the request. Identify what is required and ask why the extra data is needed.
digital-literacy.check: Share only through a verified authorized channel.

digital-literacy.title: Digital confidence plan
digital-literacy.teaching: Digital confidence grows through a repeatable task and feedback. A useful plan names one skill, a realistic practice cue, and evidence of progress.
digital-literacy.practice: Choose locating a saved resume as a two-minute practice after opening the laptop, with a fictional file.
digital-literacy.check: Success means finding and opening the right file.

email-communication.title: Email anatomy
email-communication.teaching: A message connects sender, audience, purpose, and channel. Email also has recipient and subject fields that should support that purpose.
email-communication.practice: Draft a fictional appointment request with a recipient, useful subject, requested action, and contact method.
email-communication.check: Could the recipient identify the requested action?

email-communication.title: Clear subject lines
email-communication.teaching: A subject line summarizes the matter and makes the message easier to recognize later. Vague urgency forces the reader to open the message to understand it.
email-communication.practice: Replace Help!!! with Appointment documents needed before Tuesday in a fictional draft.
email-communication.check: Does the subject accurately describe the message?

email-communication.title: Purpose-first writing
email-communication.teaching: Concise messages lead with their purpose, then supply enough context for a response. Chunking separates requests that might otherwise be overlooked.
email-communication.practice: Rewrite a long account of a missed appointment as a request, one relevant fact, and a proposed next time.
email-communication.check: Keep the request visible in the first sentence.

email-communication.title: Tone and respect
email-communication.teaching: Written tone lacks many conversational cues. Reviewing a draft after pausing can prevent a temporary reaction from becoming a lasting message.
email-communication.practice: A learner writes an angry complaint about a delay. Rewrite it using an observable fact and a respectful request.
email-communication.check: Describe behavior without assigning a motive.

email-communication.title: Attachment checks
email-communication.teaching: Proofreading includes the people and material being sent, not just spelling. An attachment should support the request and be appropriate for its recipients.
email-communication.practice: A draft says resume attached but selects the wrong file. Write a send-check covering filename, contents, and recipient.
email-communication.check: Confirm the attachment opens before sending.

email-communication.title: Links and phishing
email-communication.teaching: Audience and channel checks help expose an unexpected request. The communication slides do not establish technical phishing rules; use the lesson's security guidance too.
email-communication.practice: An unfamiliar message requests an account code. Explain choosing a known contact method to verify the request rather than replying with the code.
email-communication.check: Do not treat a familiar signature as verification.

email-communication.title: Calendar invitations
email-communication.teaching: The channel must suit the action. An invitation needs unambiguous timing and a response request so the sender can confirm understanding.
email-communication.practice: Two people interpret 7 o'clock differently. Rewrite the invitation with date, time zone, location, and reply request.

email-communication.title: Reply and reply-all
email-communication.teaching: Audience awareness includes deciding who actually needs a response. Adding recipients changes who can access the conversation and its attachments.
email-communication.practice: A group message contains one person's application details. Describe replying only to the appropriate person with minimal information.

email-communication.title: Follow-up messages
email-communication.teaching: Feedback completes communication by showing whether the message was understood. A follow-up should refer to the original action rather than assume silence means refusal.
email-communication.practice: Write a brief status request naming the original request date and asking whether more information is needed.
email-communication.check: Use the agreed response interval where one exists.

email-communication.title: Message organization
email-communication.teaching: Organization supports finding and acting on messages. Folders or categories are useful only when they connect to a clear action and review routine.
email-communication.practice: Separate a fictional inbox into Action, Waiting, and Reference; identify one message requiring a reply.
email-communication.check: A filing label does not itself complete the task.

email-communication.title: Response commitments
email-communication.teaching: A clear commitment tells the other person what to expect. If a deadline changes, an early update is more useful than silence.
email-communication.practice: Replace I'll get to it with a specific response time, then draft an update if that time becomes unrealistic.
email-communication.check: Promise only a response you can reasonably make.

email-communication.title: Video meeting readiness
email-communication.teaching: A virtual meeting is a communication channel affected by physical, psychological, and semantic noise. Reduce avoidable distractions and check the intended audience.
email-communication.practice: A participant misses instructions because the microphone is unclear. Draft a request to repeat the action and confirm it in writing.
email-communication.check: Check understanding rather than assuming agreement.

email-communication.title: Communicating a problem
email-communication.teaching: Useful feedback describes observed behavior, its impact, and a next step. Personality judgments make the issue harder to resolve.
email-communication.practice: Replace You never help with the missing file, the deadline it affects, and the specific assistance requested.
email-communication.check: Can the recipient act on the information?

email-communication.title: Professional signatures
email-communication.teaching: A signature should make it easy for the intended audience to recognize and contact the sender. Extra personal details may be unnecessary.
email-communication.practice: Create a fictional signature with name, relevant role, and appropriate contact method rather than a home address.
email-communication.check: Include only information suitable for that audience.

email-communication.title: Communication portfolio
email-communication.teaching: Communication improves through practice, feedback, and reflection. A portfolio should show what changed and why, using fictional or appropriately redacted messages.
email-communication.practice: Keep a before-and-after subject line and explain how the revision makes the request easier to understand.
email-communication.check: Assess clarity and recipient needs, not decoration.

office-documents.title: Choosing a format
office-documents.teaching: Choose the tool by the reader's task: prose explains, a spreadsheet calculates, and a presentation supports spoken delivery. Export format affects how others use the result.
office-documents.practice: Choose an editable document for a shared draft and a reviewed PDF for a fixed reading copy.
office-documents.check: Explain what the recipient needs to do.

office-documents.title: Document structure
office-documents.teaching: Heading styles create a consistent hierarchy rather than merely making text bigger. They allow related sections to be recognized and updated together.
office-documents.practice: A workplace guide uses three differently formatted titles. Assign heading levels that reflect the actual section structure.
office-documents.check: Check that equal-level headings use the same style.

office-documents.title: Formatting consistency
office-documents.teaching: A style combines formatting choices into a reusable rule. Updating a style is more reliable than manually correcting each matching paragraph.
office-documents.practice: Change the fictional guide's section-heading style once, then check all affected headings.
office-documents.check: Check for paragraphs that were formatted manually.

office-documents.title: Tables for information
office-documents.teaching: Tables organize related fields into rows and columns. Clear headers make comparisons possible; visual spacing alone does not define a dependable table.
office-documents.practice: Arrange Task, Owner, and Due date as columns in a three-row fictional action list.
office-documents.check: Can each cell be interpreted from its header?

office-documents.title: Reviewing documents
office-documents.teaching: Tracked revisions show proposed edits and reviewer actions. Turning tracking off does not automatically accept or remove existing revisions.
office-documents.practice: A draft is ready for external sharing but still contains comments. Describe reviewing each change and checking the final shared copy.
office-documents.check: Inspect comments and revision status before release.

office-documents.title: Spreadsheet cells
office-documents.teaching: A spreadsheet cell sits at a row-column intersection and can contain a value or formula. A workbook can hold multiple related worksheets.
office-documents.practice: Locate the fictional value in B3 and name its row, column, and sheet before editing.
office-documents.check: Confirm the target sheet as well as the cell.

office-documents.title: Basic formulas
office-documents.teaching: Formulas calculate from inputs, while formatting changes how a value appears. A displayed currency symbol does not turn text into a reliable number.
office-documents.practice: Explain =B2+C2 using two fictional costs, then compare the result with mental arithmetic.
office-documents.check: Check input types and the referenced cells.

office-documents.title: Sorting and filters
office-documents.teaching: Sorting changes order; filtering limits which records are visible. Related fields must stay together so a name is not separated from its amount.
office-documents.practice: A learner sorts only a name column in a payment list. Explain selecting the entire table and verifying row relationships.
office-documents.check: Compare one record before and after sorting.

office-documents.title: Readable charts
office-documents.teaching: A chart is a selected view of worksheet data. Labels, scale, and the chosen range determine what the reader can reasonably conclude.
office-documents.practice: A chart omits one month from a fictional series. Identify the range to review before commenting on the trend.
office-documents.check: Check the underlying values and axis labels.

office-documents.title: Presentation outlines
office-documents.teaching: Slides support a planned message rather than replacing the presenter. An outline connects the audience's question to a small sequence of points.
office-documents.practice: Outline a three-slide request as Problem, Proposed step, and Decision needed.
office-documents.check: Each slide should have one clear purpose.

office-documents.title: Slide readability
office-documents.teaching: Themes help keep appearance consistent, but readability still requires concise text and visible hierarchy. A crowded slide is not fixed by changing colors alone.
office-documents.practice: Turn a long paragraph into a headline and three short supporting points, leaving details for spoken explanation.
office-documents.check: Read the slide at presentation size.

office-documents.title: Speaker notes
office-documents.teaching: Speaker notes hold reminders that support delivery without crowding the slide. Notes and audience handouts serve different purposes.
office-documents.practice: Move a detailed example from a fictional slide into speaker notes, retaining the slide's central point.
office-documents.check: Check that the slide still makes sense to the audience.

office-documents.title: Exporting and sharing
office-documents.teaching: Sharing and exporting are different actions. A fixed copy should be checked after export because layout, notes, and permissions can affect the recipient's experience.
office-documents.practice: Describe opening an exported presentation PDF and checking its page order and visible notes.
office-documents.check: Verify the exact file that will be shared.

office-documents.title: Version control habits
office-documents.teaching: Review tools and file history support collaboration, but naming and location still matter. Different copies can silently contain different decisions.
office-documents.practice: Two fictional drafts are labeled final. Compare their dates and approved changes before choosing the master copy.
office-documents.check: Record who owns the next revision.

office-documents.title: Workplace project
office-documents.teaching: A workplace deliverable combines structure, calculation, and an audience-ready explanation. Review the result in the form the recipient will actually receive.
office-documents.practice: Plan a fictional one-page status report and three-slide briefing using the same verified totals.
office-documents.check: Check that numbers and dates agree across files.

it-support.title: Support roles
it-support.teaching: Information systems combine people, organizational processes, and technology. Support should ask what work is blocked rather than assuming every problem needs replacement hardware.
it-support.practice: A worker cannot complete a timesheet. Separate the device, account, process, and business task before suggesting a fix.

it-support.title: Ticket quality
it-support.teaching: Problem identification comes before solution design. A useful report distinguishes observed symptoms, affected users, business impact, and possible causes.
it-support.practice: Turn computer broken into a report naming the application, exact symptom, time, and task affected.
it-support.check: Keep observation separate from a suspected cause.

it-support.title: Reproducing issues
it-support.teaching: Critical thinking delays judgment while alternatives are examined. Reproducing an issue tests whether the same inputs and conditions create the same result.
it-support.practice: A learner reports a failed upload. Describe reproducing it with a fictional permitted file and recording the result.
it-support.check: Do not expose actual private records during testing.

it-support.title: Change one variable
it-support.teaching: Implementation includes testing and evaluating outcomes. Changing one condition makes it easier to learn which action affected the problem.
it-support.practice: A fictional app fails after two settings change. Propose a controlled authorized test of one setting with a recorded result.
it-support.check: Compare against a documented starting state.

it-support.title: Hardware basics
it-support.teaching: Hardware, software, networking, and data management are distinct technology components. An output problem can originate outside the display itself.
it-support.practice: A screen stays blank. List power, display connection, and application state as separate observations, without opening equipment.
it-support.check: Identify what is known before diagnosing a component.

it-support.title: Software installation
it-support.teaching: Outdated or unsuitable software can contribute to a business problem. Implementation also requires testing, user preparation, and a way to evaluate success.
it-support.practice: A requested application is installed from an unapproved source. Describe stopping to check authorization and the supported installation process.
it-support.check: A successful download does not establish approval.

it-support.title: User accounts
it-support.teaching: People need appropriate access, training, and organizational procedures to use a system. A login problem may involve account state or process rather than faulty hardware.
it-support.practice: A new worker lacks a role-based permission. Describe confirming the request with the authorized account owner rather than sharing a coworker's login.
it-support.check: Never collect the user's actual password.

it-support.title: Network symptoms
it-support.teaching: Telecommunications capacity and infrastructure can affect a system's ability to support work. Record the scope of a connection symptom before blaming the whole network.
it-support.practice: One fictional laptop cannot reach a service while a second can. Explain what the comparison suggests and what remains uncertain.
it-support.check: One working device does not identify the exact fault.

it-support.title: Printer troubleshooting
it-support.teaching: An information system has inputs, processing, outputs, and feedback. Following those stages can locate where a print request stops progressing.
it-support.practice: A document is queued but no page appears. Identify the application input, queued job, and printer output as separate checkpoints.
it-support.check: Use status information before repeating the job.

it-support.title: Remote support consent
it-support.teaching: Technical changes affect people and business processes. User preparation and agreed implementation steps are part of a sound solution.
it-support.practice: A technician wants remote control while the user has a private record open. Describe obtaining permission and protecting unrelated information first.
it-support.check: Consent should cover the intended support action.

it-support.title: Data handling
it-support.teaching: Raw data becomes useful information through context and processing. A support record should retain the facts needed to solve the problem without copying unrelated data.
it-support.practice: A screenshot contains an error and customer records. Describe capturing only the error details through an approved method.
it-support.check: Check that the exported image is actually redacted.

it-support.title: Escalation decisions
it-support.teaching: Solution choices depend on available resources, organizational responsibilities, and the problem's cause. Escalation is appropriate when the next action exceeds authority or evidence.
it-support.practice: A user asks an entry-level helper to change a production database. Write a factual escalation with impact and observed symptoms.
it-support.check: State the action requested and who must approve it.

it-support.title: Knowledge articles
it-support.teaching: Knowledge management helps others reuse a tested solution. A useful article includes the conditions, authorized steps, and evidence that the result worked.
it-support.practice: Draft a fictional article with Symptom, Environment, Checked steps, and Confirmed result.
it-support.check: Include the conditions where the solution may not apply.

it-support.title: Service confirmation
it-support.teaching: Feedback tells whether a system's output meets its purpose. A technician's successful test does not replace the user's confirmation of the original task.
it-support.practice: A login works but the worker still cannot submit a form. Describe checking the whole original task before closure.
it-support.check: Confirm the business outcome with the user.

it-support.title: Support portfolio
it-support.teaching: Technology supports many careers through information analysis, coordination, and decision-making. A support portfolio should show reasoning and business value.
it-support.practice: Describe a fictional ticket from symptom to verified resolution, with permissions and escalation points noted.
it-support.check: Keep credentials and identifying records out of examples.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Masonry materials
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: A masonry unit is an individual component such as brick or block; mortar bonds units into an assembly. Similar ingredients do not make mortar and concrete interchangeable.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional order asks for block and mortar. Identify each item's function before comparing products.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Site preparation concepts
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: A wall is an assembly whose supports, drainage, and connections work together. Site preparation should preserve the approved design rather than begin from appearance alone.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional crew finds the planned wall location differs from the drawing. Describe recording and clarifying the discrepancy before proceeding.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Do not redesign support details in this exercise.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Measurement and layout
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Specified, actual, and nominal dimensions describe different things. Modular layout accounts for units and joints rather than multiplying a measured unit alone.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional unit measures 7 5/8 inches with a planned 3/8-inch joint. Explain the 8-inch module used for this arithmetic example.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Do not assume every unit uses this joint size.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Mortar vocabulary
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Mortar selection depends on the assembly and required properties, not simply choosing the highest compressive strength. Workability and compatibility also matter.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional buyer proposes the strongest available mortar as a universal replacement. Explain why the project specification must decide.
masonry-fundamentals.check: An unfamiliar type requires qualified clarification.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Bond patterns
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Bond can mean a pattern, adhesion, or connection between parts. Pattern names describe arrangement and do not alone establish structural suitability.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional drawing uses staggered vertical joints. Describe the visible arrangement and ask which approved bond is intended.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Do not infer structural adequacy from the pattern alone.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Level and plumb
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Layout and assembly details work only when dimensions are interpreted consistently. TCF applies this by distinguishing level, plumb, and course alignment in the linked technical teaching.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional wall appears straight from one angle but differs from the reference marks. Describe which alignment should be checked.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Compare against the approved reference, not eyesight alone.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Tool identification
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Tools have distinct roles in mixing, carrying, placing, and finishing mortar. Naming the task first helps avoid treating similar-looking tools as interchangeable.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional learner confuses a carrying board with a joint-finishing tool. Explain each tool's intended role.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Identification is not authorization to operate equipment.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Joint profiles
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Joint profiles influence appearance and water exposure. Tooled and troweled finishes are different methods, and the specified profile governs the task.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional exterior wall shows inconsistent joint shapes. Describe the difference and the detail to check before proposing repair.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Do not choose a profile solely for appearance.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Concrete basics
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Concrete masonry units and mortar have different functions and production conditions. Concrete units develop their properties through controlled manufacture and curing.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional learner calls mortar the same thing as a block mix. Explain the distinct role each material plays.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Product similarity does not establish interchangeability.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Curing concepts
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Newly formed concrete units require controlled curing before handling and use. Early firmness is not proof that the product has reached its intended properties.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional learner wants to move a fresh unit because its surface looks dry. Identify the manufacturing guidance that should govern.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Use the product's approved curing and handling conditions.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Moisture and movement
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Masonry wall design anticipates water and movement through details such as cavities, flashing, and drainage openings. Blocking an opening can interfere with that system.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional learner proposes filling visible weep openings for a neater finish. Explain why the assembly detail should be checked first.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Do not seal an unfamiliar opening without clarification.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Quantity estimates
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Quantity estimates need a defined unit module and consistent measurement basis. Openings, approved waste allowances, and product packaging affect an order.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: For a fictional 80-inch course using an 8-inch module, calculate ten modules before discussing openings or allowances.
masonry-fundamentals.check: The example is arithmetic, not a construction specification.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Material handling
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Handling depends on product condition and an approved method. Pallet arrangement and transport planning support stability but do not remove lifting or equipment hazards.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: A fictional delivery has shifted units. Describe isolating the concern and asking for an authorized handling plan.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Do not attempt an improvised lift.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Quality documentation
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: Quality records should identify the unit, location, observed condition, and relevant drawing or specification. A photograph alone cannot establish compliance.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: Draft a fictional record of inconsistent joint profiles with location and comparison detail, avoiding an unsupported structural judgment.
masonry-fundamentals.check: Separate observation from a qualified acceptance decision.

masonry-fundamentals.title: Masonry career pathway
masonry-fundamentals.teaching: The source introduces terminology and assembly principles rather than a license to perform structural work. A career plan should connect vocabulary with supervised practice and current training requirements.
masonry-fundamentals.practice: Choose one masonry term to explain and one question to ask a qualified trainer about entry-level work.

facilities-maintenance.title: Maintenance roles
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Facilities work coordinates buildings, people, services, and business needs. Routine support and specialist technical work require different responsibilities and authorization.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional complaint about a hot room is routed to the right service rather than treated as permission to alter equipment.
facilities-maintenance.check: Identify the responsible role and business impact.

facilities-maintenance.title: Inspection versus diagnosis
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Maintenance, inspection, and testing support safe operation, but observing a condition is different from diagnosing its cause. Accurate descriptions help qualified staff decide what to do.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional stain is recorded as a ceiling mark after rain, not declared a failed pipe without evidence.
facilities-maintenance.check: Describe what was observed and what remains unknown.

facilities-maintenance.title: Work-order intake
facilities-maintenance.teaching: A help desk connects requests with response and escalation. Location, timing, symptom, impact, and a reachable contact make intake more actionable.
facilities-maintenance.practice: Turn room problem into a fictional request identifying the room, visible issue, onset, and affected activity.
facilities-maintenance.check: A clear request should reduce follow-up guessing.

facilities-maintenance.title: Prioritizing requests
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Request priority depends on safety, disruption, and the response procedure. The first request received is not automatically the most urgent.
facilities-maintenance.practice: Compare a fictional blocked exit with a cosmetic wall mark and explain why their escalation differs.
facilities-maintenance.check: Use the site's actual emergency procedure.

facilities-maintenance.title: Tool accountability
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Planned work depends on knowing which assets and equipment are present. TCF applies the asset-register idea to tool identity, location, condition, and responsibility.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional borrowed tool has no return record. Propose recording who has it and its observed condition.
facilities-maintenance.check: Do not mark an uninspected tool as ready.

facilities-maintenance.title: Routine observations
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Routine observations can reveal changes before an interruption becomes larger. A useful record identifies the location and compares conditions consistently.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional occupant reports a new vibration. Record when it occurs and what activity is affected without opening equipment.
facilities-maintenance.check: Escalate according to training and site procedure.

facilities-maintenance.title: Preventive schedules
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Preventive schedules organize inspection, testing, and maintenance before failure. Task frequency should come from the actual asset and applicable instructions, not a universal calendar.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional asset was replaced but its old schedule remains. Describe updating the register and approved maintenance plan.
facilities-maintenance.check: Confirm the current equipment identity and instructions.

facilities-maintenance.title: Energy awareness
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Environmental stewardship and efficient operation are facilities concerns. Changes intended to save energy still need to preserve safety, comfort, and the building's function.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional worker proposes turning off an unfamiliar system overnight. Identify who must verify its role first.
facilities-maintenance.check: Do not alter safety-critical equipment to save energy.

facilities-maintenance.title: Water conservation
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Operational observations can identify waste for qualified follow-up. A water-related symptom should be documented rather than treated as permission to dismantle a fixture.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional tap continues dripping after normal use. Record the location and symptom for an authorized maintenance response.
facilities-maintenance.check: Do not assume the visible point is the only cause.

facilities-maintenance.title: Cleaning compatibility
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Cleaning is planned work with tasks at different intervals. Compatibility, occupancy, and required training matter as much as completion speed.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional worker substitutes an unfamiliar cleaner to finish sooner. Describe checking the approved product and instructions instead.
facilities-maintenance.check: Never mix products based on appearance or smell.

facilities-maintenance.title: Access and emergency routes
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Space arrangements must support occupants and life safety. Moving furniture or storing supplies can affect access and emergency routes.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional delivery blocks a marked route. Describe reporting and addressing it through the site's safe procedure.
facilities-maintenance.check: Do not redesign an emergency route yourself.

facilities-maintenance.title: Contractor coordination
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Contractor coordination needs current asset information and a clear scope. An outdated register can produce an inaccurate estimate or missed work.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional contractor quotes for equipment that was removed. Identify the current asset list and work scope to confirm.
facilities-maintenance.check: Check who authorizes changes and access.

facilities-maintenance.title: Repair documentation
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Maintenance and compliance records support continuity, planning, and later review. Recording an action is different from proving every underlying requirement was met.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional work order says fixed with no detail. Add the authorized action, date, result, and follow-up need.
facilities-maintenance.check: Keep acceptance within the qualified person's role.

facilities-maintenance.title: Occupant communication
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Facilities decisions affect occupants and business activity. Updates should explain the affected service, expected next information, and any approved temporary arrangement.
facilities-maintenance.practice: A fictional room is unavailable pending review. Draft a clear update without inventing a reopening time.
facilities-maintenance.check: Report confirmed facts and the next update point.

facilities-maintenance.title: Career readiness
facilities-maintenance.teaching: Facilities careers combine communication, safety awareness, records, coordination, and technical learning. Background knowledge should lead toward supervised role-specific development.
facilities-maintenance.practice: Plan a fictional portfolio entry showing a well-documented request and appropriate escalation rather than an unsafe repair demonstration.
facilities-maintenance.check: Use fictional records and confirm current training pathways.
